questions.prompt: How is the order management system organized, and who owns what? Explain the four kinds of classes and what each holds, which domain class owns the pricing numbers and why, why OrderService is the most important service, what CustomerService keeps out of App, what StoreSnapshot is for, and what the split buys.

keyPoints.text: Domain classes represent business concepts and service classes contain business rules.
Persistence classes handle saving and loading; App handles the menu and user input.
Order owns the pricing numbers because they belong to the order.
keyPoints.quote: This class owns the pricing numbers because they belong to the order.

keyPoints.text: OrderService matters most because orders have the most business rules.
keyPoints.quote: This is the most important service because orders have the most business rules.

keyPoints.text: CustomerService keeps customer rules out of App.
keyPoints.quote: This keeps customer rules out of `App`.

keyPoints.text: StoreSnapshot simply carries the customer, product and order lists between the app and the file store.
keyPoints.quote: A simple holder object used to move lists of customers, products, and orders between the application and the file store.

keyPoints.text: Business rules are not mixed with console code, and each class has a clearer responsibility.
keyPoints.quote: the business rules are not mixed with console code

questions.prompt: How are an order's money values calculated and represented? Give the formula for a line total, how Order.recalculateTotals derives the subtotal and the total, which type holds every money value and the precision problem it avoids, and which order operations trigger a recalculation in the code.

keyPoints.text: Each item's line total is quantity times unit price.
The subtotal is the sum of all line totals.
keyPoints.quote: subtotal = sum of all line totals

keyPoints.text: The total is the subtotal minus the discount amount.
double can create tiny precision errors, such as 0.1 + 0.2 not equalling 0.3.
keyPoints.quote: `double` uses floating-point math, which can create tiny precision errors

keyPoints.text: BigDecimal is used everywhere money is involved.
keyPoints.quote: That is why this project uses `BigDecimal` everywhere money is involved.

keyPoints.text: Adding an item and removing an item each call recalculateTotals.

questions.prompt: How does the order system store its data? Name what is stored where, explain how DelimitedFileUtil writes and reads a line (which characters it escapes, which it drops, and how split decides where a field ends), what happens when the files are missing, how a save is assembled, and why ids and plain-text files were chosen.

keyPoints.text: Data lives in simple text files: customers, products, orders and order items.
keyPoints.quote: It stores data in simple text files:

keyPoints.text: DelimitedFileUtil joins fields with | and escapes special characters so names and emails do not break the format.
keyPoints.quote: It escapes special characters so names and emails do not break the file format.

keyPoints.text: escape doubles backslashes, writes | as \| and newlines as \n, removes carriage returns entirely, and turns null into an empty string.
split treats a backslash as making the next character literal (n becomes a newline); only an unescaped | ends a field.
If the files do not exist, the app starts with empty lists.
keyPoints.quote: If they do not exist, the app starts with empty lists.

keyPoints.text: On save or exit, App builds a StoreSnapshot and FileDataStore.save writes it.
keyPoints.quote: When you choose save or exit, `App` creates a `StoreSnapshot`.

keyPoints.text: Ids are UUIDs, so they stay unique without numeric counters.
keyPoints.quote: IDs use `UUID` so they stay unique without managing numeric counters.

keyPoints.text: Plain text files replace a database to keep the project understandable.
keyPoints.quote: Persistence uses plain text files instead of a database to keep the project understandable.
